title: AI Unlocked: HR & the Future of Work
blurb: For HR professionals and people leaders: recruiting and onboarding acceleration, policy and comms drafting, workforce upskilling design, the HR-AI tool market compared, and the bias/employment-law guardrails that make adoption defensible.

modules.t: People Operations in the AI Era
modules.d: Where AI strengthens HR, where it threatens fairness and trust, and how to lead the difference.
modules.body:
HR sits at the centre of the AI transition

Every organisation adopting AI is changing jobs, skills and ways of working. HR is therefore not only a user of AI tools but the function responsible for the human side of the transition: redesigning roles, reskilling people, protecting fairness and maintaining trust. HR professionals who understand AI become strategic partners; those who do not risk watching decisions about people being made without them.

The HR value chain and AI

  • Workforce planning: modelling future skill needs and scenarios.
  • Talent acquisition: job descriptions, sourcing, screening, interview design, candidate communication.
  • Onboarding: personalised plans, FAQs, document preparation.
  • Learning and development: skills assessment, personalised learning paths, content creation.
  • Performance and engagement: goal drafting, feedback support, survey analysis.
  • Employee relations and policy: policy drafting, communications, case documentation support.
  • HR operations: answering routine queries, document generation, data reporting.

The strongest uses are drafting, summarising, analysing aggregated feedback and answering routine questions. The highest-risk uses are any where AI influences decisions about individuals — who is hired, promoted, rated, disciplined or dismissed.

The decision line. AI may help HR prepare for people decisions — drafting interview questions, summarising evidence, highlighting inconsistencies. Decisions about individuals must remain with accountable humans, based on evidence, with documented reasoning and a route for the person to be heard. Many regulators now treat AI used in employment decisions as high-risk.

Fairness and bias

AI systems learn patterns from historical data. If past hiring or promotion favoured certain groups, a system trained on that data can reproduce or amplify the pattern. A widely reported example: Amazon abandoned an experimental recruiting tool after finding it downgraded CVs associated with women, because it had learned from a decade of male-dominated hiring. Bias can also arise from proxies — postcodes, schools, gaps in employment or language patterns that correlate with protected characteristics. HR must test for adverse impact, not assume neutrality.

Privacy, monitoring and trust

AI makes it technically easy to monitor employees — keystrokes, emails, sentiment, productivity scores. Excessive or covert monitoring damages trust, may breach data protection and labour law, and often measures activity rather than value. Responsible practice: be transparent about what is collected and why, collect only what is necessary, consult employees or their representatives, and never use monitoring data for decisions without human review and fair process.

Employee trust in the AI transition

Surveys consistently show many employees fear AI will threaten their jobs, while also wanting to use it to make work easier. HR can shape which feeling dominates: through honest communication, involving employees in redesigning work, investing in training, and demonstrating that time saved is reinvested in people rather than simply converted into redundancies. Trust, once lost in a transition, is very expensive to rebuild.

HR's own capability

HR teams need enough AI literacy to evaluate vendors' claims, design fair processes, advise managers and protect employees. That does not require coding — it requires understanding how AI systems learn, where they fail, and which questions to ask.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my HR transformation advisor. Ask me about my organisation's size, sector, HR team and current pain points. Map AI opportunities across our HR value chain, mark each as low, medium or high risk using the decision line, and recommend three safe starting use cases. Then draft a short, honest message to employees about how we will and will not use AI in people processes.

📚 Glossary

  • Decision line: the boundary beyond which decisions about individuals stay with accountable humans
  • Adverse impact: a selection outcome that disproportionately disadvantages a group
  • Proxy variable: a factor that indirectly reflects a protected characteristic
  • AI literacy: understanding how AI works, fails and should be governed

📖 References

  • CIPD — People profession and AI resources.
  • SHRM — AI in HR guidance.
  • Dastin, J. (2018). Amazon scraps secret AI recruiting tool that showed bias against women. Reuters.
  • European Union — AI Act (employment uses classified as high-risk).

quiz.q: The HR director of a Douala bank receiving 3,000 applications per graduate intake wants an AI system to rank candidates and reject the bottom 70% automatically, with no human review. What is the main problem?
opts: Decisions about individuals would be made with no accountable human or route to be heard
Rejecting 70% is too aggressive; the automatic cut-off should be lowered to 50% for fairness
Candidates would be rejected faster, which may harm the bank's employer brand on social
The ranking will be less accurate than recruiters, since AI cannot read CVs in French
quiz.x: The decision line keeps decisions about individuals with accountable humans and a route to be heard. Lowering the threshold (runner-up) still leaves automated rejection without review.

quiz.q: A Lagos firm's screening model, trained on ten years of hiring data, consistently scores graduates of two universities higher. What is the most likely explanation HR should test first?
opts: The model was given too little data and will correct itself as more CVs are added
Those two universities simply produce graduates who perform better in the firm's roles
The CV parser reads the formatting used by those universities more accurately
The model has learned historical hiring patterns that may not reflect job performance
quiz.x: Models reproduce past patterns, which may reflect bias rather than performance. Assuming those graduates are better (runner-up) is plausible but unproven — exactly what adverse-impact testing must check.

quiz.q: A small HR team in Kigali wants its first AI use case. Which option carries the lowest risk under the course's decision line?
opts: Flagging employees whose sick leave patterns suggest a disciplinary conversation
Drafting an onboarding FAQ from approved policies, reviewed by HR before release
Scoring video interviews for communication skills to speed up first-round screens
Producing a shortlist of internal candidates for promotion from appraisal scores
quiz.x: Drafting from approved policies with review does not influence decisions about individuals. A promotion shortlist (runner-up) looks administrative but directly shapes who gets promoted.

quiz.q: A plant manager in Accra proposes software that scores staff productivity from keystrokes and screen activity, without telling employees. What should HR advise?
opts: Proceed, provided the data is stored securely and the scores are anonymised in all reports
Proceed openly, but use the scores directly in annual ratings to keep things objective
Reject covert monitoring; any monitoring must be necessary, transparent and consulted on
Proceed for a three-month trial, then tell staff about the results once data is in hand
quiz.x: Covert monitoring damages trust and may breach law; it must be necessary, transparent and consulted on. Open use in ratings (runner-up) fixes transparency but uses activity data for decisions without fair process.

quiz.q: An HR leader in Nairobi cites Amazon's abandoned experimental recruiting tool in a board paper. Which risk does that case illustrate most directly?
opts: AI learning historical bias from past hiring data
Candidates gaming keyword filters in their CVs
AI vendors overstating the accuracy of their tools
Privacy breaches from storing applicant data
quiz.x: Amazon's tool downgraded CVs associated with women after learning from male-dominated hiring. Vendor overstatement (runner-up) is a real risk but not what the Amazon case showed.

quiz.q: Staff at a Cameroonian telecoms firm fear AI means job losses. Which HR action is most likely to build trust during the transition?
opts: Announcing that no jobs will be affected by AI for at least the next three years
Limiting information about AI plans until leadership has finalised every decision
Honest communication, involving staff in redesigning work and funding training
Offering a one-off bonus to all staff when the first AI tools are rolled out
quiz.x: Trust comes from honesty, involvement and visible investment in people. A no-job-loss promise (runner-up) is reassuring but may be impossible to keep, and broken promises destroy trust.

quiz.q: An HR business partner in Johannesburg says she will never build an AI model, so AI literacy is irrelevant to her. Why does the course disagree?
opts: She needs it because HR will soon take over AI model training from the IT department
She needs it to test vendor claims, design fair processes and advise managers
She needs it to write Python scripts that automate routine HR reporting tasks
She needs it to pass AI certification required for HR roles in most markets
quiz.x: The lesson says HR literacy is about evaluating claims, fairness and protecting employees, not coding. Scripting (runner-up) can be useful but is not the reason the course gives.

quiz.q: An analytics tool flags a high-performing engineer in Abidjan as a 'flight risk'. Her manager wants to drop her from a leadership programme as a result. What should HR advise?
opts: Agree, since programme places should go to staff more likely to stay long term
Ask the vendor to explain the score and exclude her if the reasoning is sound
Keep her in the programme but tell her the system has flagged her as a risk
Use the flag as a prompt for a career conversation, not a basis for exclusion
quiz.x: AI may prompt conversations but decisions about individuals need evidence and human judgement. Seeking the vendor's reasoning (runner-up) improves understanding but still lets a score decide her development.

quiz.q: A Ugandan HR manager is explaining the course's decision line to line managers. Which statement captures it best?
opts: AI may decide when its accuracy exceeds that of experienced line managers
AI may recommend decisions, and managers should follow unless clearly wrong
AI may help prepare people decisions; accountable humans decide on evidence
AI may make routine people decisions, while humans decide disputed cases
quiz.x: Humans decide, with documented reasoning and a route to be heard. 'Follow unless clearly wrong' (runner-up) keeps a human nominally but invites rubber-stamping.

quiz.q: A US retailer's candidate scoring model includes applicants' home postcodes. Why might this be problematic even though postcode is not a protected characteristic?
opts: Postcodes are unrelated to commute time and so add no value
It can act as a proxy for race or income, creating adverse impact
Candidates may move house, so the data quickly becomes outdated
It makes the model slower to score candidates during peak recruitment volumes
quiz.x: Proxy variables can indirectly reflect protected characteristics. Data going stale (runner-up) is a quality issue but not the fairness risk.

facts.t: Abandoned an experimental recruiting AI that downgraded CVs associated with women.
facts.more: It had learned from a decade of male-dominated hiring — historical data can encode historical bias.

facts.t: EU AI Act classification for AI used in recruitment, promotion and termination.
facts.more: Brings duties on risk management, data quality, transparency, human oversight and documentation.

facts.t: Postcodes, schools or employment gaps can stand in for protected characteristics.
facts.more: Removing names isn't enough; test outcomes for adverse impact.

facts.t: AI may help prepare people decisions; humans make them.
facts.more: With evidence, documented reasoning and a route for the person to be heard.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the productivity dashboard
plaibox.intro: You are HR lead at a 300-staff Douala logistics firm. The COO has ideas.
plaibox.win: Excellent — you protected trust, fairness and lawful process while staying a strategic partner.
plaibox.lose: Review the decision line and the monitoring principles, then try again.

steps.s: The COO wants software scoring every employee's 'productivity' from keystrokes and emails.
o: Define the business problem, then propose proportionate measures
Starts from need and proportionality, not technology.
Install it quietly so staff are not alarmed or defensive
Covert monitoring damages trust and may breach law.
Refuse outright — monitoring always erodes trust here
Closes the conversation; HR should shape a lawful approach.

steps.s: A pilot score flags 12 drivers as 'low performers'. The COO wants warnings issued.
o: Issue warnings now; the telematics data is objective
Activity data isn't value; no fair process.
Have managers review evidence and talk with each driver
Human review and the right to be heard.
Issue warnings but let drivers appeal within a week
Appeals don't fix a decision made without review.

steps.s: Rumours spread that AI will replace dispatch clerks.
o: Say nothing until plans are final, to avoid rumours
Avoids wrong promises but lets fear fill the silence.
Share what's known, what isn't, and a reskilling commitment
Honest, specific communication builds trust.
Promise nobody will lose their job, to keep morale up
A promise you may not keep destroys trust later.

modules.d: Faster, fairer hiring and better first months — with evidence-based selection at the core.
modules.body:
Start with the job, not the CV

Good hiring begins with job analysis: what outcomes the role must deliver, the tasks involved, and the competencies, knowledge and experience genuinely required. AI can draft a job analysis from interviews with the hiring manager and existing documents, but HR must challenge inflated requirements — degree requirements or years of experience that are traditional rather than necessary, which narrow the pool without improving quality.

Writing inclusive job descriptions

Job descriptions shape who applies. Research has found that gendered wording and long lists of "requirements" can discourage qualified candidates, particularly women, from applying. AI can rewrite job descriptions for clarity and inclusiveness, separate essential from desirable criteria, and translate them for multilingual markets. Check the result: the description must still accurately reflect the job.

What actually predicts performance

Decades of research on selection methods offer clear guidance. Large meta-analyses (Schmidt and Hunter's classic work, and more recent re-analyses by Sackett and colleagues) consistently find that structured interviews — the same job-related questions for all candidates, scored against predefined rubrics — are among the strongest predictors of job performance, and far better than unstructured conversations. Work samples, job knowledge tests and well-designed situational judgement tests also perform well. Unstructured interviews are prone to bias — first impressions, similarity attraction and halo effects.

AI's best contribution to selection is helping HR build structured processes quickly: job-related interview questions linked to each competency, behaviourally anchored rating scales (what a 1, 3 and 5 answer looks like), work-sample tasks, and interviewer guides. This improves fairness and prediction — the opposite of letting AI judge candidates.

Screening responsibly

High-volume screening tempts organisations to automate decisions. A responsible approach uses clear, job-related knock-out criteria (legal right to work, required licence), consistent human review against the same criteria, and — if AI tools assist — regular adverse-impact testing, transparency to candidates and human oversight. Never let AI infer characteristics such as personality or emotion from video or voice; the scientific basis is weak and the legal risk is high.

Candidate experience

Slow, silent processes lose the best candidates. AI can draft timely, personalised updates, interview scheduling messages, and respectful rejection letters. Every candidate should know where they stand. In many markets, including Cameroon, candidate experience shapes employer reputation quickly through word of mouth and social media.

Onboarding that accelerates performance

Research on organisational socialisation shows that structured onboarding improves role clarity, confidence, integration and retention. A strong onboarding plan covers four levels: compliance (policies, contracts, safety), clarification (role expectations and goals), culture (values and norms) and connection (relationships with colleagues and mentors). AI can generate a personalised 30-60-90-day plan from the job description, draft welcome materials, build an FAQ from policies, and create checklists for managers. Assign a buddy or mentor — something AI cannot replace.

Measuring hiring quality

Track time-to-hire, cost-per-hire, offer acceptance rate, candidate satisfaction, new-hire performance at six and twelve months, early attrition, and diversity at each stage of the funnel. Stage-by-stage diversity data reveals where qualified candidates are being lost.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my recruitment designer. I will describe a role. Produce: a job analysis with outcomes and essential versus desirable criteria; an inclusive job description; six structured interview questions mapped to competencies with behaviourally anchored 1/3/5 rating scales; a short work-sample task; and a 30-60-90-day onboarding plan covering compliance, clarification, culture and connection. Flag any requirement that may be unnecessarily exclusionary.

📚 Glossary

  • Job analysis: identifying a role's outcomes, tasks and required competencies
  • Structured interview: same job-related questions, scored with predefined rubrics
  • Behaviourally anchored rating scale: rating scale describing what answers at each level look like
  • Work sample: a realistic task representative of the job
  • 4 Cs of onboarding: compliance, clarification, culture, connection

📖 References

  • Schmidt, F. & Hunter, J. (1998). The validity and utility of selection methods. Psychological Bulletin.
  • Sackett, P. et al. (2022). Revisiting meta-analytic estimates of validity in personnel selection. Journal of Applied Psychology.
  • Gaucher, D., Friesen, J. & Kay, A. (2011). Evidence that gendered wording in job advertisements exists and sustains gender inequality. JPSP.
  • Bauer, T. (2010). Onboarding New Employees. SHRM Foundation.

quiz.q: A Douala logistics manager insists a junior data clerk role requires a master's degree and five years' experience. How should HR respond?
opts: Challenge whether these requirements are needed for performance, using job analysis
Keep the degree but drop the experience requirement to widen the pool by a reasonable amount
Accept them, since the hiring manager knows the role better than HR does
Ask AI to rewrite the advert so the requirements sound less intimidating
quiz.x: Job analysis tests whether requirements are necessary; inflated ones narrow the pool without improving quality. Dropping only one (runner-up) is a compromise, not evidence-based.

quiz.q: A Kenyan bank wants the selection method most supported by research for predicting job performance in relationship-manager roles. Which should it choose?
opts: Years of experience in banking as the main filter
Unstructured interviews with experienced managers
Personality profiles inferred from video interviews
Structured interviews scored on predefined rubrics
quiz.x: Meta-analyses find structured interviews among the strongest predictors. Unstructured interviews (runner-up) feel thorough but are prone to halo and similarity bias.

quiz.q: A vendor offers a Nigerian insurer an AI that scores personality from candidates' facial expressions in video interviews. What should HR do?
opts: Decline: the scientific basis is weak and the bias and legal risks are high
Pilot it on one role first and compare its scores with later performance ratings
Use it as one input alongside structured interviews to diversify evidence
Use it, provided candidates consent to the analysis before the interview
quiz.x: The lesson says not to let AI infer personality or emotion from video or voice. Using it as one input (runner-up) still feeds weak, risky evidence into decisions.

quiz.q: An HR team in Accra wants AI to improve fairness in selection for a customer-service role. Which use fits the course best?
opts: Analysing candidates' social media to assess their customer service attitude
Scoring candidates' written answers automatically to remove interviewer bias
Ranking CVs by similarity to current top performers in customer service
Building structured questions, anchored rating scales and a work-sample task
quiz.x: AI's best contribution is helping HR build structured processes quickly. Similarity to top performers (runner-up) sounds evidence-based but can replicate existing demographic patterns.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian bank's funnel data shows women are 45% of applicants, 44% of shortlisted candidates, but 15% of those passing the final interview. Where should HR look first?
opts: The CV screening criteria used to produce the shortlist
The final interview: its structure, questions, panel and scoring
The offer terms, which may be less attractive to women
The job advert wording, which may be discouraging qualified women from applying
quiz.x: The drop occurs between shortlist (44%) and final interview pass (15%). The advert (runner-up) is a common culprit but applicant share is already 45%, so it is not where women are lost.

quiz.q: A Rwandan company uses AI to generate a 30-60-90-day onboarding plan, welcome pack and FAQ. Which onboarding element should it still provide through a person?
opts: A checklist of compliance documents to sign
A glossary of company terms and acronyms
A buddy or mentor who builds relationships
A summary of the role's goals for 90 days
quiz.x: Connection through a buddy or mentor is what AI cannot replace. The 90-day goals summary (runner-up) needs manager input but can be AI-drafted.

quiz.q: A strong candidate for a Lagos fintech withdraws after three weeks without any update. Which practice would most likely have prevented this?
opts: A higher salary offer earlier in the process
An automated rejection email for other applicants
Timely, personalised updates at each stage
Fewer interview rounds for senior candidates
quiz.x: Slow, silent processes lose the best candidates; AI can draft timely updates. Fewer rounds (runner-up) helps speed but would not stop three weeks of silence.

quiz.q: A new hire at a Yaoundé NGO receives a session on her role's expectations and first-quarter goals. Which of the 4 Cs of onboarding does this address?
opts: Compliance
Connection
Culture and values
Clarification
quiz.x: Role expectations and goals are clarification. Compliance (runner-up) covers policies, contracts and safety rather than role goals.

quiz.q: An AI-rewritten advert for a Ghanaian transport company is more inclusive but now omits the legally required heavy-vehicle licence. What should HR do?
opts: Add the licence to the desirable criteria list so it does not deter applicants
Restore the licence as an essential criterion while keeping inclusive wording
Keep the new version and check licences at the offer stage to stay inclusive
Revert to the original advert, since inclusive rewrites can introduce errors
quiz.x: The description must accurately reflect the job; a legal licence is an essential knock-out criterion. Listing it as desirable (runner-up) misrepresents a legal requirement.

quiz.q: A US healthcare employer wants one metric that shows hiring quality rather than hiring speed. Which is best?
opts: New-hire performance and retention at 12 months
Offer acceptance rate for the last two quarters
Cost-per-hire compared with the industry benchmark
Average time-to-hire across all open vacancies
quiz.x: Performance and retention a year in reflect quality. Offer acceptance (runner-up) shows attractiveness of offers, not whether hires succeed.

facts.t: Structured interviews are among the strongest predictors of job performance.
facts.more: Same job-related questions, scored on predefined rubrics — far better than unstructured chats.

facts.t: Onboarding levels: compliance, clarification, culture, connection.
facts.more: Most organisations stop at compliance; connection (a buddy or mentor) is what AI cannot replace.

facts.t: Day plan that AI can draft from a job description for each new hire.
facts.more: The manager adapts it and owns the goals.

facts.t: Behaviourally anchored rating scales describe what a 1, 3 and 5 answer looks like.
facts.more: They make interviewer scoring consistent and defensible.

modules.d: Evaluating HR technology for fairness, transparency, compliance and real value.
modules.body:
An expanding and lightly tested market

HR technology vendors now attach "AI" to almost every feature. Some deliver real value; some make claims about predicting performance or culture fit that have little evidence. Because these tools affect people's livelihoods, HR must evaluate them more rigorously than ordinary software. Always verify current capabilities, evidence and legal compliance directly with vendors.

Main categories

  • General AI assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and others): drafting policies, job descriptions, communications and analysis — the most flexible and often the safest starting point when used with approved data rules.
  • Applicant tracking systems (ATS) with AI features: CV parsing, matching, scheduling and candidate messaging.
  • Sourcing tools: searching professional networks and databases for potential candidates.
  • Assessment platforms: skills tests, work samples, situational judgement tests — some with AI scoring.
  • HR information systems (HRIS) and payroll with AI assistants for employee queries and reporting.
  • Learning platforms with AI-generated content and personalised paths.
  • Engagement and survey tools analysing open-text feedback.
  • Employee service chatbots answering policy and benefits questions.

Regulation is catching up

Several jurisdictions now regulate AI in employment. New York City's Local Law 144 requires bias audits and candidate notices for automated employment decision tools. The EU AI Act classifies AI used in recruitment, promotion, task allocation and termination as high-risk, with requirements for risk management, data quality, transparency, human oversight and documentation. Data protection laws, including GDPR and many African national laws, restrict automated decision-making and require transparency. Organisations operating internationally must consider every relevant jurisdiction.

Ten questions to ask any HR-AI vendor. ① What exactly does the AI do, and what decisions does it influence? ② What evidence shows it predicts job performance? ③ Has it been independently audited for adverse impact, and can we see results? ④ What data was it trained on? ⑤ Can decisions be explained to candidates and employees? ⑥ Where is our data stored, and is it used for training? ⑦ How is human oversight built in? ⑧ How does it comply with applicable laws? ⑨ Can we export our data? ⑩ What happens when the model is updated?

Evaluation criteria

  1. Validity: evidence the tool measures what matters for the job.
  2. Fairness: adverse-impact testing across groups, ideally independent.
  3. Transparency and explainability: you can explain outcomes to affected people.
  4. Human oversight: design supports review, not rubber-stamping.
  5. Data protection and security: lawful basis, storage location, retention, training use.
  6. Local fit: languages, local labour law, payment and identity systems, connectivity.
  7. Candidate and employee experience: accessible, respectful, mobile-friendly.
  8. Integration and cost: with existing HRIS, payroll and email; total cost of ownership.

Piloting with care

Pilot high-impact tools in parallel with existing processes, comparing outcomes and adverse impact before any reliance. Inform candidates or employees as appropriate. Define success measures — time saved, quality, fairness indicators, user satisfaction — and decide based on evidence.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my HR technology evaluator. I will describe a vendor tool and how we want to use it. Assess it against the eight evaluation criteria, identify which of the ten vendor questions are unanswered, flag any regulatory classification (e.g. high-risk employment use), and design a parallel pilot with fairness and quality measures. Remind me what I must verify with the vendor directly.

📚 Glossary

  • ATS: applicant tracking system
  • HRIS: human resources information system
  • Bias audit: independent assessment of a tool's impact across groups
  • High-risk AI: EU AI Act category including many employment uses
  • Explainability: ability to explain how an outcome was reached

📖 References

  • New York City — Local Law 144 (Automated Employment Decision Tools).
  • European Union — AI Act, Annex III (employment).
  • U.S. EEOC — guidance on AI and employment discrimination.
  • CIPD — Technology and HR resources.

quiz.q: A vendor tells a Nairobi bank its AI predicts 'culture fit' from CVs but cannot show evidence linking scores to job performance. Which evaluation criterion does it fail?
opts: Data protection
Transparency
Fairness
Validity
quiz.x: Validity is evidence that a tool measures what matters for the job. Transparency (runner-up) concerns explainability, which is a separate gap.

quiz.q: A French company's subsidiary in Cameroon also hires in Belgium using an AI CV-screening tool. Under the EU AI Act, how is that tool generally classified for EU hiring?
opts: Prohibited use
Minimal-risk
High-risk
Limited-risk
quiz.x: The EU AI Act classifies AI used in recruitment as high-risk. Prohibited use (runner-up) applies to certain practices, but standard CV screening is high-risk with obligations rather than banned.

quiz.q: During due diligence on HR-AI vendors for a Ghanaian bank, four vendors answer the same questions. Which answer should most concern HR?
opts: Our model is retrained each quarter, and clients are notified before updates
Our model is proprietary, so we cannot explain scores or share audit results
Our tool supports English and French but not yet other local languages
Our data is hosted in the EU, and we can sign a data-processing agreement
quiz.x: Refusing explanation and audit results blocks validity and fairness checks. EU hosting (runner-up) may raise residency questions but is answerable with a DPA.

quiz.q: A US firm with a New York City office uses an automated employment decision tool to screen applicants. What does NYC Local Law 144 mainly require?
opts: Bias audits and notices to candidates
Human review of every single rejection
Storage of applicant data inside New York
Annual registration with the EEOC
quiz.x: Local Law 144 requires bias audits and candidate notices for AEDTs. Human review of every rejection (runner-up) is good practice but not what the law mainly mandates.

quiz.q: A Kenyan employer deploys an HRIS chatbot to answer leave policy questions. What is the most important safeguard?
opts: Limiting the chatbot to working hours so HR can monitor its answers live
Training the chatbot on past HR emails so it learns the team's usual answers
A disclaimer that answers are not binding and staff should check the handbook
Answers grounded in current approved policies, with a route to a human
quiz.x: Grounding in current approved policies with human escalation keeps answers accurate. A disclaimer (runner-up) shifts responsibility to staff without making answers correct.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian NGO is considering a European assessment platform for field-staff hiring. Which local-fit question is most relevant?
opts: Is it used by more European NGOs than the other platforms on the shortlist?
Does it support French and English, local labour law and low-bandwidth use?
Does it offer AI scoring of video answers to speed up high-volume screening?
Can it be paid for in euros under a three-year contract with a fixed price?
quiz.x: Language, local law and connectivity determine whether it works locally. Popularity with European NGOs (runner-up) says little about Cameroonian conditions.

quiz.q: A US manufacturer piloted an AI screening tool for a month without comparing it with the existing process. What should it do before deciding on rollout?
opts: Run it in parallel, compare outcomes and adverse impact, then decide
Ask the vendor for a report on the pilot results and rely on it
Roll it out, since a month without complaints shows it works well
Extend the pilot by two months and survey recruiters on usability
quiz.x: A parallel run with adverse-impact comparison gives evidence. A recruiter survey (runner-up) measures usability, not validity or fairness.

quiz.q: A Rwandan HR director asks why 'human oversight designed to avoid rubber-stamping' appears in the vendor evaluation criteria. What is the best explanation?
opts: Vendors charge extra licences for every human reviewer added
Rubber-stamping slows the process and reduces the time saved
Reviewers who just approve AI outputs give no real protection
Regulators require a set number of reviewers for each decision
quiz.x: Oversight that simply approves outputs offers no protection. The regulatory point (runner-up) sounds plausible but is not why the criterion exists.

quiz.q: A mid-sized Ugandan firm with no HR technology wants a safe starting point for AI. Which category does the course suggest?
opts: Sourcing tools that search networks for candidates
Engagement tools that analyse every employee message
General assistants for drafting under approved data rules
An AI assessment platform for scoring all applicants consistently
quiz.x: General assistants used for drafting with data rules are flexible and often safest. Sourcing tools (runner-up) are lower-risk than scoring but still touch candidate data and selection.

quiz.q: A Lagos company's ATS vendor announces a new version of its matching model. Which vendor question addresses the risk this creates?
opts: Will the new model process applications faster than the old one?
Will the update change the price of our current licence tier?
Will the interface change so that our recruiters will need retraining?
Will we be notified, and will fairness be retested after the update?
quiz.x: Model updates can change outcomes, so notification and fairness retesting are key. Retraining recruiters (runner-up) is a practical issue, not the fairness risk.

facts.t: New York City law requiring bias audits and candidate notices for automated hiring tools.
facts.more: In force since 2023 — one of the first laws aimed squarely at AI in employment decisions.

facts.t: A group's selection rate below 80% of the highest group's suggests adverse impact.
facts.more: From the US Uniform Guidelines (1978). A screening signal, not a legal conclusion; small samples mislead.

facts.t: Questions to ask any HR-AI vendor, from what it does to model updates.
facts.more: Especially: evidence it predicts performance, and independent adverse-impact results.

facts.t: GDPR article on decisions based solely on automated processing.
facts.more: Gives people rights not to be subject to such decisions with significant effects, with limited exceptions.

labs.title: Match the vendor answer to the concern
labs.intro: Each vendor reply raises one evaluation concern.
pairs: 'Our algorithm is proprietary; we can't explain scores.'
Transparency and explainability
'We've never tested results by gender or region.'
Fairness / adverse impact
'Customers love it, so it clearly works.'
Validity evidence
'Data is stored abroad and used to train our models.'
Data protection and training use
'Recruiters just click accept on the top 10.'
Human oversight
'English only; needs fast broadband.'
Local fit
labs.tip: Satisfaction is not validity; demos are not audits.

labs.title: Pilot, proceed carefully, or walk away?
items: General assistant to draft policies under data rules
Chatbot answering leave-policy FAQs, with HR escalation
ATS matching that ranks CVs for recruiters
Video tool reading 'honesty' from facial expressions
Tool predicting who will resign, used to deny promotions
labs.tip: Impact on individuals and strength of evidence decide the path.

plaibox.title: Adverse impact check (four-fifths rule)
plaibox.intro: Compare selection rates for two groups from a screening stage.

notes.t: ⚠️ Below 80% — possible adverse impact. Examine the criteria and tool before relying on it.
✓ Passes the 4/5 screen — keep monitoring; it is a rule of thumb, not proof of fairness.
Small groups make rates unstable — interpret with caution.

modules.d: Drafting compliant policies, clear communications and well-documented employee relations work.
modules.body:
Where AI helps HR communicate

HR produces large volumes of text: policies, handbooks, letters, announcements, FAQs, investigation reports and training materials. AI dramatically speeds drafting, makes language clearer and more consistent, and adapts content for different audiences and languages. The responsibility for accuracy, legality and fairness stays with HR.

Drafting policies that comply

A policy must align with applicable law — in Cameroon, the Labour Code and its implementing texts, applicable collective agreements and social security rules; elsewhere, the relevant national employment laws — as well as with the organisation's values and existing policies. AI can produce a well-structured first draft, but it may describe laws incorrectly, use another country's rules or omit local requirements. Provide AI with your actual legal requirements and existing policies, ask it to flag points needing legal verification, and have a qualified person review the final text. Policies affecting terms and conditions may require consultation with employee representatives.

The structure of a good policy

Purpose; scope (who it applies to); definitions; principles; procedures (step by step, with timelines); roles and responsibilities; related policies; consequences of non-compliance; review date and owner. Plain language is essential: a policy employees cannot understand is a policy they cannot follow.

Plain language test. Ask AI to rewrite a policy section at a reading level suitable for all staff, then to list any meaning that changed. Review the list — simplification must never alter rights or obligations.

Communications that build trust

Announcements about organisational change, restructuring or new policies shape trust. Good HR communication is honest, timely, specific about what changes and what does not, explains why, gives a channel for questions, and is consistent across audiences. AI can draft versions for staff, managers and external stakeholders, translate them, and anticipate likely questions for an FAQ. Sensitive messages — redundancies, disciplinary outcomes, bereavement — should be personal and human; AI drafts may help structure them, but the tone and delivery must reflect genuine care.

Employee relations and investigations

Employee relations cases — grievances, disciplinary matters, harassment complaints — require fair process: impartiality, the right to be heard, evidence-based conclusions, confidentiality and consistency. AI can help HR build an investigation plan, draft neutral interview questions, organise evidence chronologically and draft a report structure. AI must not determine facts, assess credibility or decide outcomes. Investigation records containing personal and sensitive data must be processed only in approved, secure tools with appropriate protections — never in public consumer chatbots.

Consistency and fairness

One valuable use of AI is checking consistency: comparing how similar cases were handled in the past (anonymised), checking whether a proposed sanction aligns with policy, and highlighting language in letters that could be perceived as biased or inflammatory. Consistency protects fairness and reduces legal risk.

Manager enablement

Managers handle most people issues first. HR can use AI to create quick guides, conversation templates and scenario practice — for example, how to respond to a request for flexible working, or how to open a performance conversation — so managers act consistently with policy and with care.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my HR policy drafter. I will give you the topic, our jurisdiction, our existing related policies and the legal requirements I have verified. Draft a policy with purpose, scope, definitions, principles, procedures, roles, consequences and review date in plain language. Flag every statement that needs legal verification. Then draft a staff announcement and a five-question FAQ for the policy launch.

📚 Glossary

  • Fair process: impartial, evidence-based procedure where people can be heard
  • Plain language: clear writing that the intended audience understands on first reading
  • Grievance: formal complaint raised by an employee
  • Consistency check: comparing treatment across similar cases
  • Collective agreement: negotiated agreement between employers and workers' representatives

📖 References

  • Republic of Cameroon — Labour Code (Law No. 92/007 of 14 August 1992) and implementing texts.
  • ILO — International labour standards and guidance.
  • ACAS (UK) — Code of Practice on Disciplinary and Grievance Procedures (good-practice reference).
  • CIPD — Employee relations guidance.

quiz.q: An AI-drafted leave policy for a Cameroonian company cites leave entitlements from French labour law. What should HR do?
opts: Keep the French entitlements, since they are usually more generous
Check each entitlement against the Cameroon Labour Code and agreements
Add a note that entitlements follow French law where not specified
Ask the AI to redraft it for Cameroon and adopt the revised version as is
quiz.x: Entitlements must be verified against the Labour Code and collective agreements. Asking AI to redraft (runner-up) may still contain errors without verification.

quiz.q: HR at a Kenyan bank uses AI to simplify its disciplinary policy into plain language. What is the most important step afterwards?
opts: Check that no rights or obligations changed in meaning
Check the reading age matches the national average for adults
Check that the new version is shorter than the old
Check the layout matches the corporate template
quiz.x: Simplification must not alter rights or obligations. Reading level (runner-up) is the goal of simplifying, not the safeguard.

quiz.q: An HR investigator in Accra is handling a harassment complaint. Which task is appropriate for an approved, secure AI tool?
opts: Organising evidence chronologically and drafting neutral questions
Recommending the sanction based on the strength of the evidence
Assessing which witness statements are more credible than others
Summarising the whole case file and stating whether harassment occurred
quiz.x: AI may organise and draft, but must not determine facts, credibility or outcomes. Summarising and concluding (runner-up) crosses into deciding facts.

quiz.q: An HR officer in Douala pastes a full harassment investigation file into a free public chatbot to get a summary. What is the main problem?
opts: The summary may be less accurate than one written by HR itself
The chatbot may not handle French and English text in one file
Highly sensitive personal data leaves approved, protected systems
The free version may truncate long files before summarising them
quiz.x: Investigation records must stay in approved, secure tools. Accuracy (runner-up) matters but the data exposure is the primary breach.

quiz.q: A Johannesburg firm is announcing a restructuring. Which announcement approach is most likely to build trust?
opts: Detailed and legalistic, so that no statement can be challenged by unions
Timely and honest, saying what changes, what does not, why, and how to ask
Brief and positive, focusing on growth opportunities rather than job impacts
Delayed until all individual outcomes are known, to avoid any speculation
quiz.x: Good communication is honest, timely, specific and gives a channel for questions. Delaying until outcomes are known (runner-up) seems careful but lets rumours fill the gap.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian manufacturer's new policy changes employees' working hours. Besides legal review, what may also be required?
opts: Publication of the policy in a national newspaper before it takes effect
Approval from the AI vendor whose tool drafted the original policy text
A vote of all employees, with the policy adopted if a clear majority agree
Consultation with employee representatives where law or agreement requires
quiz.x: Changes to terms and conditions may require consultation with representatives. An all-staff vote (runner-up) sounds democratic but is not the usual legal mechanism.

quiz.q: A Nigerian HR team wants AI to support fairness in disciplinary decisions. Which use is most appropriate?
opts: Scoring the employee's attitude from emails sent during the case
Predicting which employees are likely to face discipline next year
Drafting the final decision letter once AI has proposed the sanction
Checking consistency with policy and anonymised similar past cases
quiz.x: Consistency checks against policy and past cases protect fairness. Drafting letters (runner-up) is fine, but here AI proposing the sanction crosses the decision line.

quiz.q: A Ugandan manager must tell a long-serving employee her role is redundant. What is the best use of AI?
opts: Help structure the conversation and prepare answers; deliver it in person
Avoid AI here, as using it for sensitive matters is disrespectful to staff
Generate a script the manager reads word for word to stay legally safe
Draft and send a clear, sympathetic email so she can absorb it privately
quiz.x: AI can help structure sensitive messages, but delivery must be personal and caring. Avoiding AI entirely (runner-up) forgoes useful preparation without improving the conversation.

quiz.q: A US company's remote-work policy states the rules but not who approves requests or handles disputes. Which policy element is missing?
opts: Consequences of any breach
Purpose and scope
Roles and responsibilities
Key definitions
quiz.x: Who applies the rules is roles and responsibilities. Scope (runner-up) states to whom the policy applies, not who administers it.

quiz.q: HR at a Rwandan company uses AI to build quick guides and scenario practice for line managers. Why does the course recommend this?
opts: Guides reduce the need for HR to update policies when the law changes
Managers handle most people issues first and act more consistently with guides
AI-written guides are legally binding in a way that verbal advice is not
Managers can then make disciplinary decisions without needing to involve HR
quiz.x: Managers are the first point of contact, so guides improve consistency and care. Removing HR from decisions (runner-up) contradicts fair-process principles.

facts.t: Year of Cameroon's Labour Code (Law No. 92/007 of 14 August 1992).
facts.more: With implementing texts, collective agreements and social security rules, it frames HR policies in Cameroon.

facts.t: Structure of a good policy, from purpose to review date and owner.
facts.more: Purpose, scope, definitions, principles, procedures, roles, related policies, consequences, review.

facts.t: A policy employees can't understand is one they can't follow.
facts.more: Ask AI to simplify, then list any meaning that changed — rights and obligations must not shift.

facts.t: AI must not determine facts, assess credibility or decide investigation outcomes.
facts.more: It can help plan, draft neutral questions and organise evidence — in approved, secure tools.

labs.title: Structure the policy
labs.intro: Order the sections of a good policy.
labs.tip: Related policies can sit before consequences; the core logic flows why → who → how.

labs.title: Appropriate AI help in employee relations?
labs.intro: Sort each use in a harassment investigation.
items: Check a letter for inflammatory wording
Decide whose account is more credible
Paste witness statements into a free chatbot

plaibox.title: Simulation: the grievance
plaibox.intro: You are HR officer at a Yaoundé hospital. A nurse files a grievance against her supervisor.
plaibox.win: Fair process upheld — impartial, confidential, evidence-based, with AI in a supporting role.
plaibox.lose: Review fair process: impartiality, right to be heard, evidence, confidentiality, consistency.

steps.s: You want help planning the investigation quickly.
o: Paste the full complaint into a public chatbot
Sensitive personal data in a consumer tool.
Use the approved tool with a de-identified summary
Gets structure while protecting confidentiality.
Skip AI and plan from memory
Safe, but an approved tool could improve thoroughness.

steps.s: The AI summary calls the supervisor 'clearly aggressive'.
o: Rewrite neutrally; conclusions come from evidence
Neutral records protect fairness.
Keep it; it accurately reflects the complaint
Pre-judges the outcome.
Delete the summary and start again from scratch
Loses useful structure; editing is enough.

steps.s: Evidence is mixed. The director wants a quick decision.
o: Let AI weigh the statements to stay objective
Credibility judgements are human responsibilities.
Decide now to end the disruption
Speed shouldn't undermine fairness.
Hear both parties again and compare with past cases
Right to be heard plus consistency.

modules.d: Designing skills strategies, reskilling pathways and humane transitions as AI changes work.
modules.body:
From jobs to tasks to skills

AI rarely replaces whole jobs overnight; it changes the mix of tasks within jobs. Workforce transition design therefore starts by breaking roles into tasks and asking, for each: will AI automate it, augment it, or leave it largely unchanged? Which new tasks will emerge — reviewing AI outputs, managing data, handling exceptions, advising clients? This analysis reveals the skills each role will need and which roles will change most.

Building a skills picture

Organisations need to know what skills they have and what they will need. A skills taxonomy defines skills in consistent terms; a skills inventory records who has them and at what level. AI can help draft taxonomies, map job descriptions to skills, and analyse gaps — but self-reported and manager-assessed data should be validated, and employees should see and be able to correct their own records.

Designing reskilling and upskilling pathways

Upskilling deepens skills within a current role (an accountant learning AI-assisted analysis); reskilling prepares someone for a different role (a data-entry clerk becoming a data-quality analyst). Effective pathways combine formal learning, practice on real work, coaching and recognition. The 70-20-10 guide — most learning through experience, some through relationships, a smaller part through formal courses — reminds designers that a training course alone rarely changes capability. Build in stretch assignments, project rotations, peer learning and communities of practice.

AI literacy for everyone. Every employee now needs a baseline: what AI can and cannot do, how to use approved tools safely, how to verify outputs, data rules, and ethical considerations. Beyond the baseline, role-specific depth follows — power users, champions in each team, and specialists who build and govern systems.

Internal mobility before redundancy

When roles shrink, organisations that redeploy people into growing roles retain knowledge, loyalty and culture — and often avoid redundancy costs. An internal talent marketplace, transparent vacancy information, assessment of transferable skills and funded reskilling make mobility real. Where redundancy is unavoidable, follow the law and fair selection criteria, consult as required, and provide genuine support: notice, severance in line with law and agreements, career counselling, references and training.

Change management for the workforce

People do not resist change as much as they resist uncertainty and loss. The ADKAR model is useful here: create Awareness of why work is changing, build Desire by showing personal benefit and involving people, provide Knowledge through training, develop Ability through practice and coaching, and Reinforce through recognition, incentives and visible success stories. Line managers are the most important channel; equip them first.

Measuring the transition

Track AI literacy completion and competency, adoption of approved tools, productivity and quality indicators in redesigned roles, internal mobility rates, retention of key talent, employee confidence and sentiment, and diversity in growing roles — ensuring the transition does not leave particular groups behind.

Fairness in the transition

Workforce changes can widen inequality if reskilling opportunities go mainly to those already advantaged. Monitor who receives training and who is redeployed. Consider those with care responsibilities, limited digital access or lower formal education; design flexible, accessible learning. A fair transition is both ethical and good for long-term performance.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my workforce transition designer. I will list several roles and their main tasks. For each role, classify tasks as automated, augmented or unchanged, identify emerging tasks and required skills, and recommend upskilling or reskilling pathways using 70-20-10. Then propose an ADKAR-based change plan, internal mobility options, and metrics to monitor fairness in who benefits.

📚 Glossary

  • Upskilling / reskilling: deepening skills in a role / preparing for a different role
  • Skills taxonomy: consistent definitions of skills
  • Internal talent marketplace: system matching employees to internal opportunities
  • ADKAR: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement
  • AI literacy: baseline understanding to use AI safely and effectively

📖 References

  • World Economic Forum — Future of Jobs Report (latest edition).
  • Hiatt, J. ADKAR (Prosci).
  • Center for Creative Leadership — 70-20-10.
  • ILO — Just transition and future of work resources.

quiz.q: Leadership at a Douala insurer asks HR which jobs AI will eliminate. What is the most useful first step?
opts: Ask each manager to estimate how many of their staff AI could replace
Break roles into tasks and classify each as automated, augmented or unchanged
Freeze all hiring in administrative roles until the AI impact becomes fully clear
Benchmark against reports listing the jobs most exposed to AI globally
quiz.x: AI changes task mixes within jobs, so task analysis comes first. Global exposure reports (runner-up) give context but not the organisation's own task picture.

quiz.q: A Kenyan bank trains a data-entry clerk whose tasks are being automated to become a data-quality analyst. What is this called?
opts: Reskilling
Redeployment
Upskilling
Job enrichment
quiz.x: Preparing someone for a different role is reskilling. Upskilling (runner-up) deepens skills within the current role.

quiz.q: A Ghanaian firm's whole AI programme is one two-hour course for all staff. According to 70-20-10, what is missing?
opts: More advanced modules for technical specialists
A longer formal course with a certification exam at the end
Practice on real work, coaching and peer learning
A refresher session for all staff every year
quiz.x: 70-20-10 says most learning comes from experience and relationships. A longer course (runner-up) adds more of the 10%, not the missing 90%.

quiz.q: Analysis at a Cameroonian telecoms firm shows most staff chosen for AI reskilling are young men at head office, while women and field staff are rarely selected. What should HR do?
opts: Keep the selection, since head office roles change most with AI
Add a quota for women, leaving the field-staff gap for a later phase
Publish the figures and invite underrepresented staff to self-nominate
Investigate selection and access, and redesign for fair participation
quiz.x: HR must find the cause and redesign access fairly, including flexible learning. Self-nomination (runner-up) helps but does not fix barriers such as digital access or care duties.

quiz.q: Some finance roles at a Nigerian group are shrinking while analytics roles grow. Which approach best preserves knowledge and loyalty?
opts: Moving finance staff into analytics roles without assessment or training
Voluntary early retirement offers to the most senior finance employees
Internal mobility with transferable-skills assessment and funded reskilling
Redundancies in finance and external hiring of experienced analytics specialists
quiz.x: Funded, assessed internal mobility retains knowledge and culture. External hiring (runner-up) is faster but loses institutional knowledge and trust.

quiz.q: Staff at a Rwandan firm understand why AI is being introduced but see no benefit for themselves. Which ADKAR element is weakest?
opts: Knowledge
Desire
Awareness
Ability
quiz.x: Desire is built by showing personal benefit and involvement. Awareness (runner-up) is already present since staff understand the reasons.

quiz.q: A US retailer is planning communications for its AI workforce changes. Which group does the course call the most important channel?
opts: Their line managers
The CEO and executive team
Internal comms team
External media channels
quiz.x: Line managers are the most important channel and should be equipped first. The CEO (runner-up) sets the tone, but employees rely on their managers for what changes mean.

quiz.q: A Ugandan company has AI compile employees' skills records from their CVs and job titles. What safeguard should be added?
opts: Restrict access to HR so that managers cannot see the skills records
Add manager ratings to the records and use the average of the two scores
Have the AI rerun the analysis each quarter to keep the records current
Let employees view and correct their records, and validate assessments
quiz.x: Employees should see and correct their records, with validation. Manager ratings (runner-up) add a view but are also unvalidated and still exclude the employee.

quiz.q: A Senegalese firm wants to know whether its reskilling is producing real capability. Which metric is best?
opts: Hours of training delivered per employee compared with last year
Competency shown in redesigned roles, with quality or productivity data
Number of employees who completed the AI literacy course this year so far
Employee satisfaction scores collected at the end of each course
quiz.x: Demonstrated competency and performance show capability. Completion (runner-up) measures participation, not whether people can do the new work.

quiz.q: Redundancy becomes unavoidable for some roles at a Cameroonian bank. Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Follow the law, use fair criteria, consult as required and give real support
Select those with the lowest AI literacy scores, as these are objective data
Offer generous severance in exchange for waiving any consultation process
Announce the job cuts by email to avoid prolonged uncertainty for staff
quiz.x: Lawful, fair, consulted redundancy with support is required. AI literacy scores (runner-up) look objective but may be an unfair, unvalidated criterion.

facts.t: Learning guide: experience, relationships, then formal courses.
facts.more: A heuristic, not a law — but a reminder that a course alone rarely changes capability.

facts.t: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement.
facts.more: Prosci's model of individual change. Line managers are the key channel — equip them first.

facts.t: AI changes the task mix within jobs more often than it replaces whole jobs.
facts.more: Analyse each task: automate, augment or unchanged — and spot new tasks emerging.

facts.t: Upskilling deepens a current role; reskilling prepares for a different one.
facts.more: An accountant learning AI analysis upskills; a data-entry clerk becoming a data-quality analyst reskills.

labs.title: Automate, augment, or unchanged?
labs.intro: A Douala microfinance branch analyses its loan officer role. Sort each task.
items: Typing application data into the system
Drafting a credit memo from verified documents
Analysing a borrower's cash flow trends
Building trust with a hesitant first-time borrower
labs.tip: Then ask: which new tasks — reviewing AI outputs, handling exceptions — emerge?

modules.d: An integrated, responsible programme for AI in HR processes and the workforce transition.
modules.body:
Bringing it together

Your capstone designs a People-AI Program for your organisation (or a realistic case organisation): how HR will use AI in its own processes, and how HR will lead the workforce through AI-driven change. It must be practical, fair and compliant — something you could present to leadership next month.

Programme components

  1. Context and diagnosis: organisation, workforce profile, current HR pain points, AI adoption level and key risks.
  2. Principles: human accountability for decisions about people, fairness, transparency, privacy, and investment in people.
  3. HR use cases: three to five prioritised uses (for example structured interview design, onboarding plans, policy drafting, survey analysis), each with expected benefit, risk level and safeguards.
  4. Governance: decision line, data rules, vendor evaluation process, bias testing, documentation and oversight roles.
  5. Workforce transition plan: task analysis for key roles, skills gaps, AI literacy programme, upskilling and reskilling pathways, internal mobility.
  6. Change and communication plan: ADKAR-based actions, manager enablement, employee involvement and FAQs.
  7. Metrics: efficiency, quality, fairness, adoption, capability, employee trust and retention.
  8. Roadmap: phased 6–12 month plan with owners and milestones.
The fairness review. Before finalising, review every component with one question: who could be disadvantaged by this, and how would we know? Add a measure or safeguard wherever the answer is unclear.

Presenting to leadership

Lead with the business problem and opportunity, show the risks of unmanaged AI use (which is probably already happening), present the programme, costs and expected benefits, and request specific decisions — approval, budget, sponsors. Leaders respond to a balanced case: ambition with clear safeguards.

Your capstone deliverable

Submit a programme document of no more than eight pages plus annexes, a one-page executive summary, and one fully developed workflow (for example a structured interview kit or an onboarding plan template) with its safeguards. Your mentor reviews it for practicality, fairness, legal awareness and clarity.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my People-AI programme architect. Using what I tell you about my organisation and workforce, draft a programme with the eight components from this module, keeping it under eight pages. Then run a fairness review on each component, asking who could be disadvantaged and how we would know, and add measures or safeguards. Finish with a one-page executive summary requesting specific leadership decisions.

Going deeper — capstone playbook: your People-AI Program

Leadership will fund a programme that solves a real people problem, manages legal and fairness risk, and shows early proof. Build the capstone around evidence from your own organisation and a pilot you can describe honestly. Employment and data protection law differ by country and change; confirm current requirements with legal advisers.

Step-by-step timeline.

  • Week 1 — Diagnose. Gather workforce data (anonymised), HR process timings and pain points; survey or interview employees and managers on current AI use and concerns.
  • Week 2 — Design. Prioritise three to five HR use cases, draft governance, data rules and vendor criteria; complete task analysis for two or three key roles.
  • Week 3 — Pilot and fairness review. Pilot one use case (e.g., structured interview guide or onboarding plan); run the fairness review; collect feedback from users.
  • Week 4 — Roadmap and leadership pitch. Finalise the change plan, metrics and costs; rehearse the presentation with requested decisions.

Deliverables checklist.

  • ☐ People-AI Program document
  • ☐ Use-case prioritisation table (benefit, risk, safeguards)
  • ☐ Governance and data rules
  • ☐ Workforce transition plan with skills gaps
  • ☐ Pilot report with fairness review
  • ☐ Leadership presentation (≤ 10 slides)

Assessment rubric (weighted).

  • Diagnosis and business case — 20%: grounded in organisational evidence
  • Fairness, legality and governance — 25%: human accountability, bias testing, privacy
  • Workforce transition — 20%: credible upskilling and mobility pathways
  • Change and communication — 15%: employees involved, managers enabled
  • Pilot evidence and metrics — 20%: honest results and measurable indicators
Worked mini-example. A 250-employee microfinance institution in Cameroon finds that branch managers already use chatbots to write job adverts and that recruitment takes many weeks. The programme pilots AI-assisted structured interview guides for loan officers, with questions reviewed by HR and scored by panels, while no AI tool screens or ranks candidates. The fairness review checks that job adverts avoid gendered language and that interviews are offered in French and English. Workforce planning identifies data-entry tasks likely to shrink and creates a reskilling pathway into customer advisory roles.

Common failure modes.

  • Automating decisions about people without human accountability.
  • No employee voice in design, leading to distrust.
  • Upskilling plans with no time or budget allocated.
  • Vendor claims of "bias-free" AI accepted without evidence.
  • Metrics limited to efficiency, ignoring fairness and trust.

Submission and presentation structure.

  • 1. The business problem and current unmanaged AI use
  • 2. Principles and governance
  • 3. Priority use cases and pilot results
  • 4. Workforce transition and change plan
  • 5. Costs, metrics, roadmap and decisions requested
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a sceptical executive committee and an employee representative. Here is my People-AI Program summary: [paste]. First, as executives, challenge the costs, benefits and risks. Second, as employee representative, raise concerns about fairness, job security, surveillance and privacy. Finally, list the five strongest objections I must answer before leadership approval and suggest evidence for each.

📚 Glossary

  • People-AI Program: integrated plan for AI in HR processes and the workforce transition
  • Fairness review: checking each component for potential disadvantage and how it would be detected
  • Roadmap: phased plan with owners and milestones

📖 References

  • CIPD — Responsible AI in people management.
  • UNESCO (2021). Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence.
  • OECD — AI Principles.

quiz.q: A Douala firm's People-AI programme lists five principles. Which one most directly prevents AI from making final hiring decisions?
opts: Transparency about how AI tools are being used
Investment in people and skills for the future
Privacy and data minimisation in HR processes
Human accountability for decisions about people
quiz.x: Human accountability keeps decisions about individuals with people. Transparency (runner-up) tells candidates AI is used but does not stop it deciding.

quiz.q: During the fairness review at a Kenyan NGO, a planned AI survey analysis cannot show results by gender or location. What should be added?
opts: A larger survey sample so that the overall results are more reliable
A sentiment score so that leaders can track trends over time
Disaggregated analysis so differences between groups are visible
A vendor statement confirming that the AI tool is unbiased
quiz.x: The fairness review asks how we would know if a group is disadvantaged, which needs disaggregation. A larger sample (runner-up) improves precision but still hides group differences.

quiz.q: An HR director in Lagos is preparing to present the People-AI programme to the executive team. How should she open?
opts: With a demonstration of the AI tools HR has already been testing
With the business problem, opportunity and risks of unmanaged AI use
With the programme's eight components and the governance structure
With the budget request, so leaders know the cost from the start
quiz.x: Leaders respond to the business problem first. The budget request (runner-up) is essential but comes after the case is made.

quiz.q: A Ghanaian programme draft lists 15 HR AI use cases for year one. What is the most likely problem?
opts: Too much focus on HR's own internal processes
Too little use of AI in employee relations work
Too few use cases to justify the size of the programme budget
Too many priorities for HR's capacity and safeguards
quiz.x: The module recommends three to five prioritised use cases. Budget justification (runner-up) is the reverse of the real risk of overstretch.

quiz.q: A US firm wants one metric that captures employee trust in its People-AI programme. Which is best?
opts: Employee confidence about AI, measured over time
Number of AI tools licensed for HR this year
Reduction in HR processing time per request
Percentage of HR staff who completed training
quiz.x: Trust is shown by employee sentiment and confidence tracked over time. Training completion (runner-up) measures HR capability, not employee trust.

quiz.q: A Rwandan CEO asks why the programme needs a workforce transition plan as well as HR use cases. What is the best answer?
opts: HR use cases save too little time to justify a programme
HR use cases cannot be approved without a transition plan
HR leads people through AI changes across the whole organisation
Transition plans are required by the EU AI Act for all large employers
quiz.x: HR is responsible for the human side of organisation-wide change. Approval dependency (runner-up) is invented; the real reason is HR's role in the transition.

quiz.q: Leadership at a Cameroonian bank asks what decision is needed from them. Which request is most effective?
opts: Approve the programme, a set budget and two named sponsors
Endorse AI use in HR and let HR decide the details later
Note the programme and give feedback within the next month
Approve the concept, with budget to be discussed next year
quiz.x: Specific decisions — approval, budget and sponsors — are what the module recommends. Approving the concept (runner-up) defers the resources needed to act.

quiz.q: A Ugandan participant submits a structured interview kit annex without safeguards. What should be added?
opts: A longer set of interview questions covering more of the role's competencies
A vendor comparison of tools that could automate the kit's scoring
Data rules, review steps, fairness checks and human decision points
An executive summary describing the benefits of the interview kit
quiz.x: The workflow must include its safeguards. More questions (runner-up) improve coverage but add no protection.

quiz.q: A Nigerian company plans to buy several HR-AI tools. Which governance element addresses the risk they bring?
opts: A preference for vendors with the largest client base in Africa
An internal champion who promotes the tools to line managers
A clause letting HR cancel any vendor contract after the first twelve months
Vendor evaluation including bias testing and data protection review
quiz.x: Vendor evaluation with bias and data checks manages purchased-tool risk. A cancellation clause (runner-up) limits exposure but does not test the tool.

quiz.q: An executive at a US firm says the People-AI programme looks 'balanced'. What most likely made it so in leadership's eyes?
opts: An equal number of HR and workforce-wide initiatives
Ambition paired with clear safeguards and measurable benefits
A cautious scope that avoids using AI in any of its people processes
A low budget that keeps financial risk to a minimum
quiz.x: Leaders respond to ambition with safeguards. Cautious scope (runner-up) feels safe but abandons the opportunity the programme exists to pursue.

facts.t: Components of the People-AI Program, from diagnosis to roadmap.
facts.more: Context, principles, HR use cases, governance, transition plan, change & comms, metrics, roadmap.

facts.t: Prioritised HR use cases, each with benefit, risk level and safeguards.
facts.more: Fewer, well-governed use cases beat many unmanaged ones.

facts.t: Horizon of the phased roadmap, with owners and milestones.
facts.more: Leaders respond to ambition with clear safeguards.

facts.t: UNESCO adopted its Recommendation on the Ethics of AI.
facts.more: Endorsed by its member states — a global reference for fairness, transparency and human oversight.

labs.title: Which programme component?
labs.intro: Place each item in the People-AI Program.
items: Bias testing before any screening tool is used
Training participation by gender and site
Employee trust score in pulse surveys
labs.tip: Every component should answer: who could be disadvantaged, and how would we know?

labs.title: Review this draft executive summary
labs.intro: Tap the statements that would weaken the case to leadership.
segments: Staff are already using AI tools informally, with no data rules.
We propose three HR use cases: interview kits, onboarding plans and policy drafting.
AI will fully automate hiring decisions, cutting recruiter costs by 90%.
Crosses the decision line and quotes an unsupported figure.
Every use case has a named owner and safeguards.
Fairness reviews are unnecessary because the tools are neutral.
Tools are not neutral by default; fairness must be tested.
We will roll out to all 12 sites in the first month.
Unrealistic; a phased 6–12 month roadmap with pilots is expected.
We request approval, a budget and an executive sponsor.
labs.tip: Balanced, specific, honest — and asking for clear decisions.
